hubs.title: Getting around
hubs.tagline: One console for every certificate, CA and job that needs a person.
hubs.intro: Sign in, see what needs attention today, and jump to any certificate, CA or setting from the keyboard. The console works the same on a phone.

hubs.intro: Create a root and the issuing CAs under it, or import a root you already trust. Sensitive operations on a CA are guarded, and a new root key can require an M-of-N key ceremony.

hubs.title: Windows and Active Directory
hubs.tagline: Autoenrollment for domain machines and users, without an ADCS server.
hubs.intro: Kryptkeeper serves MS-XCEP and MS-WSTEP natively, so domain-joined Windows machines and users enroll through Group Policy with Kerberos, exactly as they did with ADCS. Templates say whether they are offered to machines or users, ADCS templates can be imported, and a Windows agent and WinRM scanning cover the machine stores.

points.title: Group Policy autoenrollment
points.text: Point the domain's enrollment policy at Kryptkeeper. Machines and users authenticate with Kerberos and enroll and renew on their own. Proven on Windows 11 and Server 2022.

points.title: Templates for machines or users
points.text: Each template says whether Windows offers it to computer accounts or to users, and which groups may enroll.

points.title: Move off ADCS gradually
points.text: Import your ADCS templates, run both CAs side by side, and let old certificates expire naturally.

hubs.intro: Templates fix key types, lifetimes and approvals. Issuance policies add rules on top, can be drafted from plain English, and can be dry-run against a request before they go live.

hubs.title: Build your own integrations
hubs.tagline: Plugins, an API and SDKs, so Kryptkeeper fits your stack.
hubs.intro: If Kryptkeeper doesn't support a device yet, write a delivery plugin for it. Plugins are WebAssembly modules that run sandboxed in the hub, declare exactly what they may touch, and are signed so you can tell first-party, verified and community plugins apart. Everything in the console is also available over a documented REST API, with SDKs, a Terraform provider and an MCP server.

points.title: Write a plugin in three functions
points.text: Start from the example plugin and implement Validate, Push and Rollback. The hub checks what the device actually serves, so a plugin cannot claim success it didn't earn.

points.title: Sandboxed and least privilege
points.text: A manifest declares whether the plugin receives private keys and which hosts it may reach. The hub refuses anything undeclared, and new plugins start disabled.

points.title: Signed and tiered
points.text: Plugins signed with the Kryptkeeper key are first-party, plugins signed by a publisher you trust are verified, and unsigned ones are community.

points.title: First-party plugins to copy
points.text: AWS (ACM, ALB, CloudFront), Azure (Key Vault, App Gateway, Front Door), HashiCorp Vault, cloud secret managers, Cloudflare, F5 and Citrix ship as plugins built on the same SDK.

points.title: API, SDKs and Terraform
points.text: Go, Python and TypeScript SDKs, a Terraform provider and an MCP server sit on the same REST API the console uses.

points.title: Events out
points.text: Webhooks, ITSM tickets and SIEM forwarding (CEF) carry every alert and security event to your own tools.

hubs.title: What's new in 1.1
hubs.tagline: Keep your CA, trust it everywhere, and get ahead of post-quantum.
hubs.intro: Version 1.1 lets you issue through the CA you already run, push its roots to your hosts with a second person's approval, install onto SQL Server, Remote Desktop and Exchange over WinRM, and plan post-quantum waves with a target algorithm. These walkthroughs show each screen that exists in the console today; what 1.1 does not do yet is on the roadmap.
